body: The shared pattern: trading or leveraged money early, survival through the 1992 boom-bust on the bear side, then a pivot to long-held conviction positions bought during pessimism. Each fortune is ultimately dominated by one asset: D-Mart for Damani, which he built, and Titan for Jhunjhunwala, which he bought. The timing (entering about 1985-86 at the start of India's multi-decade re-rating), the network and survivorship are large non-replicable components.

`case_study:shopify-2015-2025` · tickers US-SHOP · confidence: verified

IPO May 2015 at $17 (10:1 split June 2022 -> ~$1.70). Rose ~6,480% to the Nov 2021 peak (~$169-176 split-adj) as the 'arms dealer' to independent merchants; Merchant Solutions (Shopify Payments, Capital, Shipping) overtook subscriptions — take-rate on GMV, not seats. Crash: 2022 bear market + post-COVID e-commerce normalisation + a capex-heavy logistics push (Deliverr bought for $2.1bn in 2022) returned Shopify to losses; stock -87% to $23.63 (Sept 2022). Reset: 10% layoffs July 2022, then May 2023 20% layoffs and sale of logistics/Deliverr to Flexport for a ~13% stake; stock +27% that day. Back to asset-light: positive operating income for 9+ quarters, FCF margins mid-teens+ [unverified]. New all-time high in late Oct 2025 (surpassing 2021; C$253 on TSX); 2025 was described as its best year. Split: 2015-21 mostly multiple on fast revenue; 2023-25 mostly margins/FCF growth. EARLY SIGNAL visible 2016-18: Payments attach rate rising, Plus enterprise merchants, app-ecosystem revenue — platform economics; in 2023 the signal was management abandoning capex-heavy logistics. Who caught it: founder Tobi Lütke (controlling shares); Baillie Gifford and other growth funds [unverified]. LESSON: a platform that drifts into capital-intensive operations loses its multiple; reversing that drift is itself a buy signal, and recovery to new highs took ~4 years.

- **Start → end:** ~$1.70 split-adj (IPO $17) → ~$169-176 (Nov 2021); new ATH Oct 2025 (~100x IPO->2021)
- **EPS vs rerating:** 2015-21 multiple-heavy; 2023-25 margin/FCF
- **Max drawdown:** -87% (Nov 2021-Sep 2022)
- **Early signal:** payments attach, Merchant Solutions > subscriptions; 2023 logistics exit
- **Who caught it:** Tobi Lütke; growth funds [unverified]
- **Ended/stalled:** recovered to new highs Oct 2025
- **Lesson:** platforms lose multiple when they go capital-heavy; reversal is the signal
- **Sources:** [1](https://www.fool.com/investing/2022/07/27/down-80-shopify-stock-exits-nosebleed-territory) · [2](https://thelogic.co/news/why-axis/shopify-unloads-logistics-business-to-flexport-in-major-strategic-shift-as-it-cuts-20-of-workforce/) · [3](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/shopify-stock-good-investors-091500785.html) · [4](https://www.fool.ca/2025/11/14/3-reasons-shopify-stock-could-set-a-new-all-time-high-in-2026/) · [5](https://www.modernretail.co/technology/why-2025-was-shopifys-best-year-yet/)

`case_study:amazon-1997-2021-compounding` · tickers US-AMZN · confidence: verified

IPO May 1997 at $18. Splits 2:1 (1998), 3:1 (1999), 2:1 (1999), 20:1 (2022) = 240x: IPO ≈ $0.075 on today's basis. Dot-com peak Dec 1999 ~$107 nominal (~$4.4 adj) -> Sept 2001 ~$5.5 (~$0.28 adj): -94%. July 2021 peak ~$3,770 pre-2022-split (~$188): ~2,500x from IPO; ~670x from the 2001 low [split math mine]. Split: EPS was near-zero/negative for years by design; the driver was operating cash flow and later AWS profits; P/E is not meaningful. EARLY SIGNAL visible 1997-2002: the 1997 shareholder letter ('It's all about the long term', optimise for FCF per share, not GAAP EPS), negative working-capital cycle (paid by customers before paying suppliers), and customer counts compounding; Prime (2005) and AWS (2006) were later hidden segments — AWS was first broken out only in 2015, revealing a highly profitable cloud business. Who caught it: Bill Miller (Legg Mason) bought at the IPO, re-entered ~$88 pre-split in the late 1990s, and doubled down near ~$6 in 2001 after a -93% fall, reasoning the book business generated FCF with little inventory risk (247wallst); Nick Sleep/Qais Zakaria (Nomad, from ~2005) [unverified]. Ended/stalled: 2021 peak then -56% in 2022 (see case_study:amazon-drawdown). LESSON: the right metric can differ from EPS (FCF/share, unit economics); a founder willing to reinvest at scale and a hidden segment (AWS) can deliver 1,000x+, but only to holders who survive a -94% drawdown.

- **Start → end:** $18 IPO = ~$0.075 split-adj → ~$188 split-adj (Jul 2021) (~2,500x)
- **EPS vs rerating:** FCF/AWS-driven; P/E not meaningful
- **Max drawdown:** -94% (1999-2001)
- **Early signal:** 1997 letter (FCF/share focus), negative working capital, customer growth; AWS disclosure 2015
- **Who caught it:** Bill Miller (doubled down ~$6 in 2001); Nick Sleep/Nomad [unverified]
- **Ended/stalled:** 2021 peak, -56% 2022
- **Lesson:** right metric + founder reinvestment + hidden segment; survive -94%
- **Sources:** [1](https://www.cnbc.com/2018/12/18/dotcom-bubble-amazon-stock-lost-more-than-90percent-long-term-investors-still-got-rich.html) · [2](https://www.irishtimes.com/business/personal-finance/amazon-s-wild-ride-offers-lessons-for-investors-1.3099248) · [3](https://247wallst.com/investing/2026/10/01/by-2001-his-amazon-shares-had-fallen-93-and-wall-street-was-predicting-the-company-would-go-bankrupt-bill-miller-didnt-care-he-doubled-down-at-6-a-share-two-decades-later-he-had-more-amazon-sto/) · [4](https://www.fool.com/investing/2017/03/22/how-much-money-would-i-have-if-i-had-invested-at-a.aspx)

body:
| Finding | Paper | What it means for us |
|---|---|---|
| Firms that **change** their 10-K/10-Q text from the prior year underperform. The short-"changers", long-"non-changers" portfolio earned up to 188 bp/month (about 22%/yr) when changes were in the risk-factor section; typical value-weighted figures are 34–58 bp/month. Returns build over up to 18 months with **no announcement reaction**, so investors are inattentive. Changes in CEO/CFO, litigation and negative-sentiment wording predict the most. | Cohen, Malloy & Nguyen, "Lazy Prices", *J. Finance* 75(3) 2020, 1371–1415 ([NBER w25084](https://www.nber.org/papers/w25084), [digest](https://www.nber.org/digest/nov18/are-investors-inattentive-sec-mandated-corporate-reports)) | Diff every Indian annual report (MD&A, risk, contingent liabilities, RPT notes, auditor's report) and every concall against the prior one. Most changes are boring; flag *unusual* change size. This is exactly an AI-at-scale task, and Indian small caps get even less attention than US firms. |
| General dictionaries misclassify finance words: about 3/4 of Harvard-IV "negative" words are not negative in 10-Ks. The LM finance-specific negative list (2,337 words) correlates with filing returns, volatility, fraud and material weakness. Fog is a poor readability measure in finance; file size is a better proxy. | Loughran & McDonald, *J. Finance* 2011 ([SSRN](https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=1331573)); L&M readability paper | Use the LM word lists (or an LLM) for tone, never generic sentiment. Track "uncertainty" and "weak modal" word counts over time *within the same company*. |
| Firms with lower earnings write longer, harder-to-read annual reports; easier-to-read reports go with more persistent positive earnings. | Li, "Annual report readability, current earnings, and earnings persistence", *JAE* 45 (2008) 221–247 ([RePEc](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jaecon/v45y2008i2-3p221-247.html)) | A sudden rise in length or complexity of the MD&A or concall answers is a yellow flag. |
| Conference-call tone predicts abnormal returns and volume, and outweighs the earnings surprise over the following 60 days (US). | Price, Doran, Peterson & Bliss, *J. Banking & Finance* 36(4) 2012 ([RePEc](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jbfina/v36y2012i4p992-1011.html)) | Tone carries information in the US... |
| **India:** 8,273 BSE-500 concall transcripts (559 firms, 2004–2019). Optimistic tone lifts short-window returns but **does not predict future operating performance**; retail investors respond most to the tone. | Jain, Khizer & Thirumalai, "Textual Disclosures and Retail Investors" ([NYU Stern PDF](https://www.stern.nyu.edu/sites/default/files/assets/documents/Jain%20Khizer%20Thirumalai%20-%20Textual%20Disclosures%20and%20Retail%20Investors.pdf), [NSE white paper](https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/s3fs-public/inline-files/Retail%20Investors%20and%20Textual%20Disclosures%20-%20Jain%2C%20Khizer%20and%20Thirumalai%20-%20White%20Paper.pdf)) | ...but **in India, cheerful tone is cheap talk.** The edge is not tone scoring. It is **checking what was promised against what was delivered**. Bullish-tone-with-poor-delivery companies may be systematically overpriced. |
| Complex call language is part obfuscation and part genuine information. Analysts' own question complexity can serve as the benchmark for the legitimate part. | Bushee, Gow & Taylor, *JAR* 56(1) 2018 ([RePEc](https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/joares/v56y2018i1p85-121.html)) | Score management *non-answers*: did the answer address the question? An LLM can judge this directly. |
| Deceptive CEOs/CFOs (later restatements) use more general-knowledge references ("you know", "everybody knows"), fewer shareholder-value references and fewer non-extreme positive words; CEOs use more *extreme* positive words. Models beat random by 6–16%, and the most-deceptive-CFO portfolio had −4% to −11% annual alpha. | Larcker & Zakolyukina, *JAR* 50(2) 2012 ([HLS forum](https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/2012/03/21/detecting-deceptive-discussions-in-conference-calls/)) | A cheap red-flag feature: superlatives ("tremendous", "fantastic") plus evasion. Weak on its own, so use it only as one input. |
| Negative vocal affect on calls predicts misses of consensus over the next 3 quarters. | Mayew & Venkatachalam, *J. Finance* 67(1) 2012 ([Duke](https://www.fuqua.duke.edu/duke-fuqua-insights/vocal-cues-influence-company-performance)); the LVA software was **criticised as unreliable** (Lacerda) | Interesting but fragile. Indian REC mp3s exist (screener links), but this is low priority. |
| Managers with accurate past forecasts get larger analyst revisions and price reactions to new guidance. Bad-news forecasts are more credible than good-news ones. | Williams (1996, *TAR*); Hutton & Stocken (2009 WP, [Wharton](https://rodneywhitecenter.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2014/04/0207.pdf)); Rogers & Stocken (2005, *TAR*) | Credibility is a **measurable track record**, and the market prices it. Few people measure it for Indian small caps, because guidance is informal and lives only in concall text. That is our gap. |
